title: Revenue depends on one or a few customers
why_funders_care: If one buyer leaves, pays late or squeezes prices, the company's ability to repay or grow can collapse. Receivables lenders often cap how much they will advance against any single debtor.
warning_signs: Largest customer accounts for more than about 20-25% of revenue
Top 3-5 customers account for most of sales
Receivables ledger dominated by one debtor
No written contracts with the main customers
mitigations: Diversify into new customers, channels or regions and track concentration monthly
Put the key relationships under multi-year written contracts
Use credit insurance or ask for lender-approved concentration limits
Show the creditworthiness and payment record of the main buyers
evidence_to_prepare: Revenue by customer for the last 2-3 years
Key customer contracts and payment history

sources.title: Invoice Finance - some typical facility terms explained
sources.supports: Explains that invoice finance lenders apply concentration limits on any one debtor, that 'the more concentrated your ledger the greater the risk', and that 20% is a standard limit for many providers.

sources.title: Into The Lender's Mind #11: The risk of customer concentration and how to dilute it
sources.supports: Practitioner newsletter describing a bank red-flagging a profitable company because it had one customer; it offers rule-of-thumb thresholds (e.g. largest customer above 25% of revenue) and mitigations. Informal source, not an official guideline.

sources.title: Credit Risk I: Sample Loan Policy Outline (FDIC guidance outline for loan policies)
sources.supports: Sample loan policy outline lists 'Concentrations of Loans' (including common source of repayment) as a topic lender policies address; general support only, at portfolio level rather than borrower level.

title: Too little operating or credit history
why_funders_care: Lenders rely on past performance and repayment behaviour to judge risk; young firms have short credit histories and new borrowers default more often in some portfolios.
warning_signs: Company trading for less than 2-3 years
No prior loans or repayment record with any lender
Fewer than two years of filed accounts or tax returns
Recent change of business model or ownership
mitigations: Start with a smaller or shorter facility to build a repayment record
Use founders' track record, guarantees or a credit guarantee scheme
Bring in a co-lender or supplier credit with a record
Report to credit bureaus where available
evidence_to_prepare: All available historical accounts and management accounts
Repayment history on any prior loans, supplier credit or leases
Founder CVs showing relevant prior experience

sources.title: MSME Finance Gap: Assessment of the Shortfalls and Opportunities in Financing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Emerging Markets
sources.supports: States that younger firms face particular difficulty 'because they have shorter credit histories and typically do not have established relationships with lenders'.

sources.title: Pathways to Prosperity: Rural and Agricultural Finance State of the Sector Report
sources.publisher: ISF Advisors and Mastercard Foundation Rural and Agricultural Finance Learning Lab
sources.supports: Reports from a lender portfolio analysis that 'new borrowers' risk of default was twice as high as that of existing borrowers' in agri-SME lending.

sources.title: Can I get a loan after three to five years of trading in the UK?
sources.publisher: Start Up Loans Company (British Business Bank)
sources.supports: British Business Bank subsidiary notes that trading history 'shows stability, experience, and proven performance' and that a few years of accounts can help an application.

title: No audited or reliable financial statements
why_funders_care: Funders need credible financial information to assess risk; where independent, credible accounts are missing, lenders face information asymmetry and either decline or price higher.
warning_signs: Only unaudited or internally prepared accounts
Accounts prepared mainly for tax purposes and differing from management figures
Auditor not independent or with limited standing
Late or missing statutory filings
mitigations: Commission an audit or at least a review by a reputable independent accountant
Adopt a consistent accounting framework and monthly close
Reconcile tax, statutory and management accounts
Explain any qualified audit opinions
evidence_to_prepare: Audited or reviewed financial statements for 2-3 years
Reconciliation of statutory vs. management figures

sources.title: Financing SMEs in a context of strong information asymmetry (J. Lefilleur, Private Sector & Development)
sources.supports: Describes a lack of 'independent, competent and credible accounting firms' in Sub-Saharan Africa as affecting 'the quality of financial information transmitted to banks', which it calls a main stumbling block to SME finance.

sources.title: Empirical study on financial information and cost of finance in Serbia (SME financial reporting quality)
sources.publisher: World Bank (Centre for Financial Reporting Reform)
sources.supports: World Bank study finds SME financial reporting quality is inversely related to the cost of debt (modest effect, about 24-33 basis points per standard deviation); it does not test audit status itself.

sources.title: SME Finance
sources.supports: Notes that the quality and reliability of SME financial statements 'varies across countries and firms' and that MSMEs often lack capacity to prepare sound statements.

title: Informal, incomplete or inconsistent records
why_funders_care: Informal firms cannot document cash flows or ownership, so formal lenders largely cannot serve them; poor record keeping is cited as an internal risk factor by agri lenders.
warning_signs: Business not formally registered or licences lapsed
Sales recorded in cash with no bank trail
Numbers differ between pitch deck, accounts and bank statements
Personal and business transactions mixed in one account
mitigations: Register the business and run all revenue through a business bank account
Adopt simple bookkeeping software and keep receipts
Reconcile records monthly to bank statements
Consider mobile-money or digital payment trails as evidence

sources.title: MSME Finance Gap: Assessment of the Shortfalls and Opportunities in Financing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Emerging Markets
sources.supports: States that 'the amount of formal lending to informal firms is close to zero' and that MSMEs find it difficult to ensure transparency about their creditworthiness.

sources.title: Pathways to Prosperity: Rural and Agricultural Finance State of the Sector Report
sources.publisher: ISF Advisors and Mastercard Foundation Rural and Agricultural Finance Learning Lab
sources.supports: Lists 'internal factors such as poor management capacity and record keeping' among reasons financial institutions perceive high risk in agri-SME lending.

sources.title: Financing SMEs in a context of strong information asymmetry (J. Lefilleur, Private Sector & Development)
sources.supports: Says most SMEs operate informally and often cannot provide the basic information banks require.

title: Not enough acceptable collateral
why_funders_care: Banks often use collateral as a secondary source of repayment and to offset information gaps; many SMEs lack assets of the type and value lenders accept.
warning_signs: Few fixed assets or assets without clear title
Land held under customary or unregistered title
Requested loan far exceeds pledgeable asset value
Assets already pledged to other lenders
mitigations: Use movable collateral (equipment, inventory, receivables) where a registry exists
Seek a partial credit guarantee from a DFI or national scheme
Use cash-flow or contract-based lenders, e.g. purchase order or receivables finance
Offer personal or corporate guarantees where appropriate
evidence_to_prepare: Asset register with valuations and title documents
Details of any guarantee scheme eligibility

sources.title: MSME Finance Gap: Assessment of the Shortfalls and Opportunities in Financing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Emerging Markets
sources.supports: States that 'MSMEs find it difficult to provide high-quality collateral at all times' and lists high collateral requirements among terms that discourage applications.

sources.title: The Trade Finance Program and Its Role in Lifting Impediments to Trade (ADB Briefs No. 82)
sources.supports: Reports that trade finance rejections were mainly attributed to inability to meet standard bank requirements, including collateral (47% of respondents).

sources.title: Financing SMEs in a context of strong information asymmetry (J. Lefilleur, Private Sector & Development)
sources.supports: Says collateral is often a prerequisite for loans, which 'excludes the majority of entrepreneurs', and that mortgages are hard to enforce in Sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Cash flow too thin to cover repayments
why_funders_care: Lenders' primary repayment source is operating cash flow; if cash flow does not comfortably exceed scheduled debt service, the loan is unaffordable.
warning_signs: EBITDA or operating cash flow below 1.1-1.25x annual debt service
Recent losses or volatile margins
Existing debt repayments already absorb most cash flow
Repayment relies on projected rather than historical cash flow
mitigations: Ask for a smaller amount, longer tenor or grace period matched to cash generation
Restructure or refinance expensive existing debt
Raise equity alongside debt
Show seasonal cash-flow profile and align repayments to it
evidence_to_prepare: DSCR calculation on historical and projected cash flow
Monthly cash-flow forecast for loan tenor
Debt schedule of all existing obligations
Sensitivity analysis on sales and margins

sources.title: Best Practices: SOP 50 10 8 Update - New 7(a) Small Loan Underwriting Requirements
sources.supports: Law-firm summary of SBA SOP 50 10 8 stating that for 7(a) Small Loans the DSCR 'must be equal to or greater than 1.1:1 on an historical and/or projected cash flow basis'.

sources.title: The 5 C's of Credit
sources.supports: SBA lender describes 'Capacity' as 'a measure of your ability to pay the lender back', comparing income to expenses and asking for two years of filed taxes and interim financials.

sources.title: Small business finance: what today's lenders look for
sources.supports: UK accountants' guide says lenders want evidence that 'dependable cash flow and consistent profits show you can afford repayments'.

title: Already too much debt relative to equity
why_funders_care: High existing debt leaves little capacity to absorb shocks and reduces the owner's stake at risk; lenders look for meaningful owner capital ('skin in the game').
warning_signs: Debt-to-equity or debt-to-EBITDA well above sector norms
Negative or very thin net worth
Shareholder loans used instead of equity
Little owner cash contribution to the project being financed
mitigations: Convert shareholder loans to equity or subordinate them
Raise new equity or quasi-equity before adding senior debt
Retain earnings rather than distribute
Show owner contribution to the project

sources.title: SBA SOP 50 10 8 Lender and Development Company Loan Programs (copy hosted by Coleman Report)
sources.supports: SBA SOP 50 10 8 lists 'leverage ratio' among examples of 'other factors' (with credit history and management experience) that lenders may consider as credit weaknesses.

sources.title: The 5 C's of Credit
sources.supports: SBA lender explains 'Capital' as 'how much skin you are willing to put in the game', noting banks often look for a 30% down payment (CDC: 10%, 20% for startups).

title: Borrowing in hard currency but earning in local currency
why_funders_care: A devaluation can sharply raise the local-currency cost of hard-currency debt for a business with local revenues, a known driver of debt distress.
warning_signs: USD/EUR loan requested by a business with mainly local-currency sales
No natural hedge (exports or hard-currency pricing)
History of sharp local currency depreciation
No hedging plan or budget
mitigations: Seek local-currency lending or hedged products (e.g. via TCX-backed lenders)
Match currency of debt to currency of revenues
Price contracts in or index them to hard currency where legitimate
Stress-test repayments under devaluation scenarios
evidence_to_prepare: Revenue and cost breakdown by currency
Hedging quotes or local-currency term sheets

sources.title: African Development Bank approves equity investment in the Currency Exchange Fund (TCX) to support access to local currency financing across Africa
sources.supports: AfDB says its TCX investment aims to 'mitigate the foreign exchange risks faced by borrowers in Africa' and reduce 'the mismatch between the currency of debt and revenue for local borrowers', including MSMEs.

sources.title: Key Financing Policy Reforms and Solutions for the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development
sources.supports: Recommends DFIs expand access to currency hedging platforms and local-currency capital for local capital providers serving small and growing businesses.

title: Deal is too small for the funder
why_funders_care: Due diligence and monitoring costs are similar for small and large deals, so small tickets can be uneconomic; many DFIs and funds have explicit minimum ticket sizes.
warning_signs: Amount sought is below the funder's stated minimum
Need is in the $20k-$2m 'missing middle' range but approaching large DFIs directly
High due-diligence cost relative to deal size
mitigations: Target funders whose ticket range fits (local capital providers, small business funds, SME banks)
Access large DFIs indirectly via their funds or on-lending partners
Combine needs into a larger, staged facility only if justified
evidence_to_prepare: Clear statement of amount and staging
Shortlist of funders with matching ticket ranges
Standardised data room to lower due-diligence cost

sources.title: The Missing Middles: Segmenting Enterprises to Better Understand Their Financial Needs (Summary Report)
sources.publisher: Collaborative for Frontier Finance / Omidyar Network / Dalberg
sources.supports: States that 'transaction costs for very small ticket financing often exceed the income that financial service providers can obtain' and that many dynamic enterprises are not large or high-yielding enough to justify those costs.

sources.title: Partner with us
sources.supports: Norfund states equity tickets 'from USD 5-50 million' and loans from USD 5 million, illustrating DFI minimum ticket sizes.

sources.title: Financing SMEs in a context of strong information asymmetry (J. Lefilleur, Private Sector & Development)
sources.supports: Says information asymmetry raises transaction costs and, because SME loan amounts are small, creates 'a problem of economies of scale'.

title: Company's stage or growth profile does not fit the funder
why_funders_care: Funders target particular stages and growth profiles; applying venture-capital expectations to moderate-growth or asset-heavy businesses, or bank criteria to pre-revenue ventures, creates mismatch.
warning_signs: Pre-revenue company seeking bank debt
Steady, moderate-growth business pitching to VCs
Asset-heavy model with long payback approaching funds with short horizons
Requesting growth equity before product-market fit
mitigations: Identify which enterprise segment you are and target matching capital
Consider revenue-based finance, mezzanine or blended capital for moderate-growth firms
Use grants or early-stage risk capital before seeking debt

sources.title: The Missing Middles: Segmenting Enterprises to Better Understand Their Financial Needs (Summary Report)
sources.publisher: Collaborative for Frontier Finance / Omidyar Network / Dalberg
sources.supports: Segments SGBs into high-growth ventures, niche ventures, dynamic enterprises and livelihood-sustaining enterprises with different needs, and identifies a mismatch from applying 'Silicon Valley' VC growth and timeline expectations to asset-heavy ventures.

sources.title: Key Financing Policy Reforms and Solutions for the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development
sources.supports: Describes the 'missing middle' of SGBs 'too large for microfinance and too small or risky for PE/VC investments and banks'.

title: Weak governance and controls
why_funders_care: Weak governance raises risks of fraud, regulatory non-compliance and value loss; DFIs and impact investors assess governance and integrity alongside financials.
warning_signs: No board, or board made up only of founders/family
No financial controls, segregation of duties or approval limits
Unclear decision rights between owners and managers
No conflict-of-interest policy
mitigations: Set up an advisory board or board with at least one independent member
Adopt basic financial controls and delegation of authority
Introduce a conflicts-of-interest and related-party policy
Hold and minute regular board meetings

sources.title: IFC Family Business Governance Handbook (2nd edition)
sources.supports: Cites a study that 'an active and outside (non-family-controlled) board was the most critical element' for long-lived family firms, and says investors highly value board, shareholder-rights and disclosure practices.

sources.title: Governance red flags in venture capital start-ups: interpreting and acting on warning signs
sources.supports: BII guidance says weak governance can lead to fraud, regulatory non-compliance, financial and impact losses and reputational damage, and that investors should proactively identify governance red flags.

sources.title: VC Governance Guidance Note
sources.supports: FMO note says investors should 'help founders shape governance and internal controls as the company grows' and that 'gaps are typically only addressed when issues arise'.

title: Business depends on one person
why_funders_care: If the founder holds all relationships, knowledge and decisions, illness, departure or death could stop the business; succession is a well-known weakness of founder- and family-run firms.
warning_signs: Founder signs all contracts and holds all key relationships
No deputy, successor or documented processes
No key-person insurance
Founder also personally guarantees most obligations
mitigations: Develop a second line of management and delegate authority
Document processes and customer relationships
Put a succession plan in place
Consider key-person life/disability insurance

sources.title: IFC Family Business Governance Handbook (2nd edition)
sources.supports: Notes '95 percent of family businesses do not survive the third generation of ownership' and that founders 'should make the necessary efforts to plan for their succession', warning many put it off until the last minute.

sources.title: How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions? (Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan, Strebulaev)
sources.publisher: NBER conference paper / Harvard Business School et al.
sources.supports: Survey of VCs finds the team is the top driver of both success (96%) and failure (92%); general support for funders' focus on people, not specifically on single-person dependence.

title: Management team lacks depth or relevant experience
why_funders_care: Investors rate the management team as the most important selection factor, and lenders treat poor management capacity as a risk driver.
warning_signs: No finance lead or CFO-type role
Key roles held by family members without relevant skills
Team lacks industry experience
High turnover of senior staff
mitigations: Hire or contract a qualified finance manager
Add advisors or non-executive directors with sector experience
Set merit-based roles and pay for family members
Show a hiring plan funded by the raise

sources.title: How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions?
sources.publisher: Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance
sources.supports: Reports the management team was mentioned as important by 95% of VC firms and as the most important factor by 47%.

sources.title: How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions? (NBER Digest)
sources.supports: Says 'VCs view the quality of the management team as more important than the business model, product, or market', valuing ability, industry experience and passion.

sources.title: Pathways to Prosperity: Rural and Agricultural Finance State of the Sector Report
sources.publisher: ISF Advisors and Mastercard Foundation Rural and Agricultural Finance Learning Lab
sources.supports: Lists 'poor management capacity' among internal factors behind lenders' high perceived risk in agri-SME lending.

title: Tax arrears or regulatory non-compliance
why_funders_care: Unpaid taxes signal cash strain and create liabilities that can rank ahead of lenders or trigger penalties; lenders often ask for tax clearance.
warning_signs: Outstanding VAT, payroll or corporate tax
No valid tax clearance/compliance certificate
Expired licences or permits
Ongoing disputes with regulators
mitigations: Agree a payment plan with the tax authority and stick to it
Obtain a current tax clearance certificate
Renew licences and keep a compliance calendar
Disclose any disputes upfront with legal assessment
evidence_to_prepare: Tax authority statement of account and payment plan

sources.title: Small business finance: what today's lenders look for
sources.supports: UK accountants state that unpaid tax liabilities such as VAT or Corporation Tax 'are a major red flag to lenders'.

sources.title: Why SARS Compliance Matters for SMEs Seeking Business Funding
sources.supports: South African SME guide says lenders use SARS records as a key indicator, that tax debt 'suggests potential financial instability', and that without a path to compliance most applications are declined; lists a valid Tax Clearance Certificate among documents.

sources.title: SBA SOP 50 10 8 Lender and Development Company Loan Programs (copy hosted by Coleman Report)
sources.supports: SBA SOP 50 10 8 states operating company financial statements 'are subject to tax verification'; general support that lenders verify figures against tax records.

title: Environmental, social or governance standards not met
why_funders_care: DFIs and many impact investors require clients to identify and manage environmental and social risks to recognised standards such as the IFC Performance Standards.
warning_signs: No environmental and social policy or management system
Labour issues (no contracts, unsafe conditions, child or forced labour risk in supply chain)
No grievance mechanism
Pollution, land or community impacts not assessed
mitigations: Adopt an E&S policy and a management system proportionate to risk
Run an E&S risk assessment and action plan
Set up worker and community grievance mechanisms
Train staff on health and safety and labour standards
evidence_to_prepare: Health & safety records and HR policies

sources.title: IFC Performance Standards on Environmental and Social Sustainability
sources.supports: PS1 requires clients to establish an Environmental and Social Management System, policy, risk identification, stakeholder engagement and grievance mechanism; PS2 covers labour conditions including child and forced labour and occupational health and safety.

sources.title: Norfund Risk Appetite Statement
sources.supports: Norfund states it must minimise 'risks related to environmental, social and governance (ESG) compliance, as well as climate risk at investee level'.

sources.title: Root Capital: partnering with small and growing agribusinesses to address social and environmental challenges
sources.publisher: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)
sources.supports: Notes Root Capital runs impact due diligence including a 'negative screen' for practices that could harm communities or the environment.

title: Business activity is on a funder exclusion list
why_funders_care: DFIs and their intermediaries will not finance activities on their exclusion lists (e.g. weapons, tobacco, gambling, certain alcohol), regardless of financial strength.
warning_signs: Revenue from weapons, tobacco, gambling, spirits or other listed activities
Products banned under host-country law or international conventions
Use of forced or harmful child labour
Commercial logging in primary tropical moist forest
mitigations: Check each target funder's exclusion list early
If the activity is ancillary, quantify and ring-fence it
Target funders whose mandate permits the activity
evidence_to_prepare: Statement of compliance with exclusion lists

sources.title: IFC Exclusion List (2007)
sources.supports: Lists excluded activities including weapons and munitions, tobacco, alcoholic beverages (except beer and wine), gambling, unbonded asbestos fibres and illegal products; ancillary activities may be exempt, and financial intermediaries must also exclude forced/harmful child labour.

title: Unclear or unjustified use of funds
why_funders_care: Funders need to know exactly what the money will pay for, so they can judge whether it generates the cash to repay or the growth to return capital.
warning_signs: Request for a round number with no breakdown
Funds partly to repay owners or old debts without explanation
Mismatch between instrument and purpose (e.g. short-term loan for long-term capex)
No link between spending and revenue impact
mitigations: Provide an itemised use-of-funds table with quotes
Tie each spend to milestones and revenue or cost impact
Match instrument tenor to the asset or need financed
evidence_to_prepare: Business plan section linking spend to returns

sources.title: Start your journey
sources.publisher: Better Business Finance (supported by UK Finance and UK banks)
sources.supports: UK industry guidance says lenders 'will want to understand how you plan to use the finance you have requested' (premises, equipment, stock, cash flow).

sources.title: Credit Risk I: Sample Loan Policy Outline (FDIC guidance outline for loan policies)
sources.supports: Sample loan policy outline calls for a statement of the 'Purpose of loan' in applications and 'Acceptable types of loans and purposes' in policy.

title: Projections look unrealistic
why_funders_care: Funders discount forecasts that diverge sharply from history or sector norms; investors report that most portfolio companies miss their projections.
warning_signs: Hockey-stick revenue growth with no supporting pipeline
Margins far above sector peers
Projections inconsistent with historical accounts
No downside scenario
mitigations: Build forecasts bottom-up from pipeline, capacity and pricing
Benchmark against peers and history
Show base, upside and downside cases
State key assumptions explicitly
evidence_to_prepare: Track record of past forecast vs actual

sources.title: How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions? (Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan, Strebulaev)
sources.publisher: NBER conference paper / Harvard Business School et al.
sources.supports: Reports that fewer than 30% of VC portfolio companies meet their projections (26% early-stage, 33% late-stage).

sources.title: Small business finance: what today's lenders look for
sources.supports: Warns against 'asking for unrealistic amounts of funding' and says 'sudden spikes in revenue or costs will raise questions - lenders like stability'.

sources.title: Start your journey
sources.publisher: Better Business Finance (supported by UK Finance and UK banks)
sources.supports: Says lenders may ask for financial forecasts to see where the business is heading and that a cash-flow forecast helps a responsible lender minimise the risk of missed repayments.

title: No credible exit for equity investors
why_funders_care: Equity investors must return capital to their own investors; where IPOs are rare and buyers are few, they need a credible route to sell their stake.
warning_signs: No identifiable strategic or financial buyers
Minority stake with no exit rights
Founders unwilling to consider sale or buy-back
Business too small or founder-dependent to be sold
mitigations: Identify likely acquirers and comparable transactions
Offer structured exits (buy-backs, revenue-based redemption, put options)
Professionalise management and systems to make the business saleable
Consider self-liquidating instruments instead of pure equity

sources.title: The answer to the 'exit challenge' in Africa (A. Caude, Adenia Partners)
sources.supports: Reports 'limited exit opportunities' were named by 76% of LPs as the biggest challenge for Africa fund managers and that none of 33 African PE exits in the prior year was via IPO.

sources.title: How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions? (Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan, Strebulaev)
sources.publisher: NBER conference paper / Harvard Business School et al.
sources.supports: Finds exit considerations are the top factor VCs use in valuation (86% important) and reports an average exit mix of 15% IPO, 53% M&A, 32% failure.

sources.title: The Missing Middles: Segmenting Enterprises to Better Understand Their Financial Needs (Summary Report)
sources.publisher: Collaborative for Frontier Finance / Omidyar Network / Dalberg
sources.supports: Notes that many SGBs lack the return and exit prospects venture capitalists seek.

title: Valuation expectations out of line with investors
why_funders_care: Investors price deals off exit prospects, comparables and target ownership; an asking valuation that cannot deliver their required return blocks the deal.
warning_signs: Valuation based on headline multiples from other markets
Small equity stake offered for a large amount
No comparable transactions to support price
Valuation not linked to cash flows or exit value
mitigations: Benchmark against regional comparable deals
Show the investor's path to target return
Consider instruments that defer valuation (convertibles, SAFEs, revenue-based finance)
Be flexible on structure rather than headline price

sources.title: How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions? (Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan, Strebulaev)
sources.publisher: NBER conference paper / Harvard Business School et al.
sources.supports: Finds VCs value deals mainly via exit considerations and comparables, require on average 31% IRR and about 5.5x cash-on-cash, and that valuation matters more for late-stage investors.

sources.title: How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions?
sources.publisher: Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance
sources.supports: Reports valuation ranked fifth overall among selection factors but third for later-stage deals.

title: Exposure to commodity prices and seasonal cash flows
why_funders_care: Price swings and seasonal harvest cycles create volatile cash flows; lenders see climate and price volatility as major risks in agricultural lending.
warning_signs: Single commodity dominates revenue
Fixed-price sales contracts with no hedge
Repayment schedule not aligned with harvest
Large stock held through price swings
mitigations: Align repayments to the harvest and sales cycle
Use price-indexed contracts or hedging where available
Diversify crops or products
Hold stock only against confirmed sales

sources.title: Pathways to Prosperity: Rural and Agricultural Finance State of the Sector Report
sources.publisher: ISF Advisors and Mastercard Foundation Rural and Agricultural Finance Learning Lab
sources.supports: Cites 'external factors such as climate change and price volatility' as reasons lenders perceive high risk in agri-SME lending.

sources.title: Improving coffee farmer welfare with innovative credit solutions in developing countries (Blouin, Macchiavello, McCreless)
sources.supports: Finds a 10% unexpected coffee price rise raises default probability by almost three percentage points on fixed-price contracts, and that fixed-price contracts alone do not provide price insurance.

sources.title: Our Expertise
sources.supports: Root Capital describes seasonal loans 'tailored to your harvest and sales cycles', showing repayment alignment to seasonal cash flow.

title: Supply shortfalls or side-selling
why_funders_care: Where loans are repaid from sales to a specific buyer, farmers or enterprises selling elsewhere when prices rise can cause strategic default.
warning_signs: Aggregator relies on farmers without supply agreements
History of failing to deliver contracted volumes
Spot prices often exceed contract prices
No tracking of supplier deliveries
mitigations: Strengthen supplier relationships (pre-finance, services, prompt payment)
Use price-indexed contracts
Track deliveries and loyalty by supplier
Use tripartite buyer-enterprise-lender arrangements

sources.title: Improving coffee farmer welfare with innovative credit solutions in developing countries (Blouin, Macchiavello, McCreless)
sources.supports: Describes loans from buyers as 'susceptible to side-selling' when prices rise and estimates 'roughly half of the observed defaults are strategic'; notes bundling buyer, enterprise and lender relationships reduces this risk.

title: No firm offtake or export contract
why_funders_care: Contract-based lenders use signed sales contracts or purchase orders from creditworthy buyers in place of hard collateral; without them, repayment is uncertain.
warning_signs: Sales based on informal or spot buyers
No purchase orders from established buyers
Buyer creditworthiness unknown
Contract terms not assignable to a lender
mitigations: Secure written offtake agreements or purchase orders
Build relationships with established buyers and get references
Agree payment through a lender-controlled account
Use letters of credit where appropriate
evidence_to_prepare: Signed offtake/export contracts or purchase orders

sources.title: Root Capital: partnering with small and growing agribusinesses to address social and environmental challenges
sources.publisher: International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)
sources.supports: Says Root Capital 'uses businesses' sales contracts to mitigate risk, rather than insisting on the collateral', pre-finances using purchase orders from international buyers, and requires 'strong relationships with established buyers'.

sources.title: Improving coffee farmer welfare with innovative credit solutions in developing countries (Blouin, Macchiavello, McCreless)
sources.supports: Describes lending models where buyer, enterprise and lender relationships are bundled so the buyer contract underpins repayment.

title: Country, political or transfer risk
why_funders_care: Foreign banks and investors factor in a country's credit rating, political stability and FX convertibility; poor country ratings constrain cross-border finance regardless of company quality.
warning_signs: Operating in a low-rated, fragile or sanctioned country
History of FX controls or transfer restrictions
Dependence on a weak local bank for letters of credit
mitigations: Use DFI guarantees or political risk insurance
Work with confirming banks or DFI trade finance programmes
Hold revenues offshore where legal (exporters)
Target funders whose mandate includes your country

sources.title: The Trade Finance Program and Its Role in Lifting Impediments to Trade (ADB Briefs No. 82)
sources.supports: Reports country credit rating (82%) and issuing bank rating (85%) among reasons banks cited as impediments to trade finance.

sources.title: Norfund Risk Appetite Statement
sources.supports: Norfund lists 'Country & political risk' as a risk it accepts under its mandate, citing Sub-Saharan Africa and LDCs, showing it is a recognised underwriting dimension.

title: Unclear ownership or beneficial owners
why_funders_care: Regulated funders must identify and verify the natural persons who ultimately own or control a borrower; if they cannot, they may refuse or exit the relationship.
warning_signs: Shares held by nominees or offshore entities without disclosure
Share register out of date or not matching registry filings
Undocumented verbal ownership arrangements
Complex group structure with no organogram
mitigations: Update the share register and registry filings
Prepare a beneficial-ownership declaration down to natural persons
Provide a group structure chart with percentages
Certify foreign documents via lawyer/notary
evidence_to_prepare: Certificate of incorporation, memorandum and articles
Register of members / official registry extract

sources.title: Guidance on Beneficial Ownership
sources.supports: Requires banks to identify beneficial owners (more than 10% ownership, control, or senior managing official), lists documents to collect, and says banks may need to end relationships in high-risk cases where ownership cannot be established.

sources.title: The Trade Finance Program and Its Role in Lifting Impediments to Trade (ADB Briefs No. 82)
sources.supports: Reports AML/KYC (90%) as the top regulatory reason banks cited as an impediment to trade finance.

title: Related-party dealings or mixing personal and business money
why_funders_care: Commingled funds and undisclosed related-party transactions make cash flows unreliable and can divert value from the company and its funders.
warning_signs: Business assets used for owners' personal needs
Purchases from or sales to owner-related companies without arm's-length terms
Loans to or from directors without documentation
Personal and business payments in one bank account
mitigations: Separate personal and business accounts
Adopt a related-party transaction policy with board approval
Document and price related-party dealings at arm's length
Disclose related parties to funders

sources.title: IFC Family Business Governance Handbook (2nd edition)
sources.supports: Contrasts 'Family First' firms where business resources may be used 'for family members' personal needs (housing, cars, personal purchases, etc.)' with 'Business First' firms with 'a clear separation of business and family assets', and requires directors to disclose conflicts of interest.

title: Market too small for the funder's return target
why_funders_care: Venture investors need large markets to generate outsized returns; businesses with limited addressable markets may be good companies but poor fits for VC.
warning_signs: Serviceable market small relative to amount raised
Growth plan depends on capturing an implausible share of market
No credible expansion path beyond a niche
mitigations: Size the market bottom-up with credible data
Show adjacent markets or geographies
Target funders suited to niche or moderate-growth businesses

sources.title: The Missing Middles: Segmenting Enterprises to Better Understand Their Financial Needs (Summary Report)
sources.publisher: Collaborative for Frontier Finance / Omidyar Network / Dalberg
sources.supports: Describes niche ventures whose growth tapers because the addressable market has limited upside, and a mismatch from 'applying venture capital scale expectations to businesses with smaller addressable markets'.

sources.title: How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions?
sources.publisher: Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance
sources.supports: Reports 68% of VC firms cite market as an important selection factor.

title: Missing KYC/AML documents
why_funders_care: KYC and anti-money-laundering requirements are among the most-cited reasons banks reject transactions, especially in trade finance; incomplete documents stall or end applications.
warning_signs: Missing IDs or proof of address for directors/owners
Inconsistent company names or numbers across documents
Unexplained source of funds
Counterparties in high-risk jurisdictions
mitigations: Prepare a complete KYC pack before approaching funders
Keep registry records current
Document source of funds and wealth
Screen own counterparties for sanctions
evidence_to_prepare: Certified IDs of directors and beneficial owners

sources.title: The Trade Finance Program and Its Role in Lifting Impediments to Trade (ADB Briefs No. 82)
sources.supports: Reports regulatory reasons for trade finance rejections including AML/KYC at 90%, and client-side issues including documentation (37%) and valid company records (34%).

sources.title: Trade Finance Gaps Continue Despite Fintech Breakthroughs
sources.supports: Lists know-your-customer (KYC) concerns, additional collateral and low margins among reasons for rejected trade finance transactions; only 20% of rejected deals were considered unbankable.

sources.title: Business integrity (impact specialism page)
sources.supports: BII describes business integrity risk management as covering 'financial crime, regulatory and reputational risks' and requires investees to implement its integrity risk requirements.

title: Poor or missing credit history of the business or owners
why_funders_care: Lenders check business and personal credit histories as a proxy for willingness to repay; where credit bureaus are weak, missing history also counts against applicants.
warning_signs: Past defaults, arrears or write-offs
Low business or personal credit score
Unresolved judgments
No bureau record at all
mitigations: Obtain and correct your credit report
Settle or restructure outstanding arrears
Build history with small facilities repaid on time
Provide supplier and landlord references

sources.title: The 5 C's of Credit
sources.supports: SBA lender says 'Character' is 'essentially your credit history', with lenders weighing personal credit scores.

sources.title: Start your journey
sources.publisher: Better Business Finance (supported by UK Finance and UK banks)
sources.supports: Says lenders run a credit check on the business, or personally for sole traders and partnerships.

sources.title: Financing SMEs in a context of strong information asymmetry (J. Lefilleur, Private Sector & Development)
sources.supports: Notes that in Sub-Saharan Africa 'credit bureaus either do not exist or are ineffective', so banks lack tools to check new clients' payment behaviour.

title: Exposure to climate and weather shocks
why_funders_care: Weather shocks can destroy production and repayment capacity, and DFIs increasingly assess climate risk at investee level.
warning_signs: Rain-fed production in drought- or flood-prone areas
Single-site operations exposed to extreme weather
No insurance
No adaptation measures
mitigations: Take up index or crop insurance where available
Diversify sourcing locations
Invest in irrigation, storage or other adaptation
Include weather scenarios in forecasts

sources.title: Pathways to Prosperity: Rural and Agricultural Finance State of the Sector Report
sources.publisher: ISF Advisors and Mastercard Foundation Rural and Agricultural Finance Learning Lab
sources.supports: Cites climate change among external factors that make financial institutions perceive high risk in agri-SME lending.

sources.title: Norfund Risk Appetite Statement
sources.supports: Norfund states it seeks to minimise ESG compliance risks 'as well as climate risk at investee level'.

title: Loan tenor too long for the lender's comfort
why_funders_care: Longer loans to SMEs carry more uncertainty; in agri-SME portfolios, loans over 12 months were far more likely to fall into arrears.
warning_signs: Multi-year loan requested by a young or seasonal business
Working-capital need financed with long-term debt
Asset life shorter than the requested tenor
mitigations: Match tenor to the asset life or cash cycle
Split need into short-term working capital and medium-term asset finance
Use leasing or asset finance for equipment

sources.title: Pathways to Prosperity: Rural and Agricultural Finance State of the Sector Report
sources.publisher: ISF Advisors and Mastercard Foundation Rural and Agricultural Finance Learning Lab
sources.supports: Reports that 'loans with tenors of more than 12 months were over four times more likely to fall into arrears' in the agri-SME portfolio analysed.

sources.title: OECD Financing SMEs and Entrepreneurs Scoreboard: 2025 Highlights
sources.supports: Notes SMEs are shifting toward smaller, short-term financing amid a restrictive environment; general context only.

title: Company falls outside the funder's mandate
why_funders_care: DFIs and funds invest only in defined countries, sectors and instruments; applications outside the mandate are usually not pursued regardless of quality.
warning_signs: Sector not among the funder's priority sectors
Country outside eligible list (e.g. not ODA-eligible)
Requested instrument or ownership stake not offered
mitigations: Read each funder's stated sectors, geographies, ticket sizes and instruments before applying
Approach the funder's fund or bank partners if direct investment is out of scope
evidence_to_prepare: One-page fit summary mapping the company to the funder's criteria

sources.title: Partner with us
sources.supports: Norfund invests in ODA-eligible developing countries in defined sectors, with a maximum 35% equity stake, and says submissions outside its scope 'will generally not be followed up further'.
